Zithulele Hospital

By: Nicola De Chaud | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A flailing rural hospital is turned around on the passion of a young team of doctors

Summary:
Ten years ago, Zithulele hospital in the remote eastern cape area was falling apart. The hospital served a marginalized population of around 300 000 people and it had only 2 permanent staffers. A young newly graduated couple on a mission took it on, and turned it around. Through their pioneering approach, and passionate staying power, they today run a first class institution, with a full complement of staff and drastically improved statistics for health in the area. This is their heartfelt story

Further information:
This programme is already produced. It is agreed that it will be re-edited with further emphasis on the lives of the central couple.

Press Release:


Zithulele’s Medical Miracles **NEW INSERT**
Ten years ago Zithulele hospital, located in the remote Eastern Cape, was falling apart. The hospital serves a marginalized population of around 300 000 people and had, at the time, only 2 permanent staff members. Then a newly graduated couple looking for a place to serve arrived with a pioneering approach and passion sufficient to lure 18 colleagues to the rural outpost. Carte Blanche meets the doctors who have put down roots in the humble community and made Zithulele a first class medical facility.


Script:


Zithulele Script

Ben: It’s an incredible privilege to serve people and to do so often in their hour of need. Especially in this part of the world people don’t have access to other health services so we’re it. So it gives me a kick and it’s a great place to live.

VO: Zithulele hospital is on the Wild Coast, in deep rural eastern cape. It is perched on rolling coastal hill at the end of a long dusty potholed road 4 hours from he nearest city.

Tarryn:I always wanted to work in a rural area, somewhere in Africa. I chose medicine so I could work in a rural area and give of myself in some way.

VO: In 2005 Ben and his wife Tarryn were newly qualified doctors looking for a place to serve.

Ben: There was a real shortage of staff here, and they said we want you to go to Zithulele and we said ‘whooo where’s Zitulele, what’s Zithulele?”

VO: Zithulele was a run down dysfunctional district hospital.

Ben: But we came and we literally spent two hours here and we met the friendly staff and we just knew it was the right place for us.

VO: The staff was made up of 1 radiographer and 3 interns, and they were straining to serve a community of 130000 people

Ben: Ja, we literally spent two hours here and felt it was the right place

Tarryn: When we first came here it we were the only older couple, we had one child at the time. We really felt like pioneers pioneering our way

VO: They took on a desperately understaffed hospital, straining to serve a community of 130 000 people

Ben: When we started out we had a sense of a dream of what we hoped to see happen here. We had some strategies, but in some ways we fell into this adventure and have tried to make wise decisions as we go along

Tarryn: We came with guns blazing, many times where we threw things and shouted and said,’this is how it must be!” and the passion’s changed over the years

Ben: A piece of advice from a professor that we regard as a mentor gave us was, if you intend to stay for 10 years, tell people that from the beginning, because they will treat you differently. And we did that and we quickly realized it’s gonna take about 10 years to get this hospital running smoothly like the kind of hospital we’d like to work in.

CEO: The clinical manager, the fair one who came in i205, with the vision that we want to take this hospital somewhere

Ben: We set out not knowing how we were going to achive the dream but really working off the premise that there are people out there who want to do good things and if we can create the context for that to happen then hopefully those other people will come and join us

VO: They were first joined by med school colleagues, Karl and Sally le Roux

Karl: We said to them we would be more than happy to commit five years to help yo establish this dream, we think it would be much easier if you did it with a core group of 5 rather than just the two of you

VO: The four put down roots and have made a life for themselves and their families as part of the community.

Tarryn: Building a house in the community, that was really putting roots down. Our oldest son Joshua had i=his first birthday when we got here and we have two other children born to this community, who have only known this community and then we have Abanati whom we’ve adopted.

Sally: The community is incredible and it really feels like we are making changes here

VO: The team approaches each daily challenge with a commitment to maintaining a hopeful attitude

Ban: When you are faced with a challenge – either expected or unexpected, that quite frankly you should not be facing, you can either throw your hands up in the air and say woe is me I can’t handle this or you can try and find a solution

CEO: but today we are where we are because of the teamwork with the clinical management so that we make sure we attract and retain staff.

VO: Over the years they have attracted a strong group of dedicated health practitioners to the faraway hospital on the hill.

CEO: We’ve go so many physiotherapist, occupational therapists, things we couldn't dream of, we have audiometric, someone who cares for ears o which some time ago it was a dream

Tarryn: I feel like it was our dream, and people have taken it on as their dream and I feel like that’s an amazing gift for us. I am in awe of the people who work alongside us.

Nurse: I’ve been here since 2007. I love babies, I lost my baby, he was five months and was mismanaged. I didn’t know anything about babies, how are babies sick, how can I identify that, so wherever I go my interest is with the little ones. Ok I do love mums, but not so much, my interest is with the little ones

There is change on so many different levels. We’ve seen a massive increase in the number of deliveries for example


VO: Zithulele doubled the delivery of healthy babies in 10 years.

Ben: We’ve managed to achieve a decrease in the perinatal mortality rate which is obviously really important to us. Child health likewise.

VO: The Gaunt’s have overseen a massive turnaround though their decade at Zithulele.

Ben: I summarize my job as making it possible for other people to do their jobs

Tarryn: I like to tell people that my main job at the hospital is to be a juggler

VOP: Tarryn juggles her time between the hospital and home, where she is also a part time teacher

Tarryn: What I currenltyu do is homeschool my children in the morning

Ben: Its not just about schooling it’s about being engaged with the world and the community around us

VO: Committment to the community is the bedrock of their approach. Zithulele hospital staff visit local clinics and make regular home visits

OT: We try to go out as much as we can and on the sway to the clinic do a home visit. Home visits are you opportunity to really understand where a patient is coming from, that look on their face when they see that they are being cared for. It’s like rally being alive.

Ben: We put it on our website that we were originally a mission hospital and continue in that ethos, and that's true, people here care about patients, and really see them as people.
The thing that really brings joy is making a difference to peoples lives, sometimes that’s a small thing or big and dramatic like saving lives, but whether it’s big or small it’s about making a difference to individuals lives and letting them know that they are valued./














Promo’s


Zithulele hospital on the remote hills of the wild Coast is an unexpected beacon of hope


In the face of a huge shortage of rural doctors, a young couple beats the odds.


Access to health care is a struggle for most rural South Africans.... Zithulele Hospital is a surprising gem, perched on the hills of the wild coast
